mark_split.label: Reduce to a function of the new variable

insider_note: Checking a1/a2 = b1/b2 first is what tells a student to use the linear substitution v = a1x + b1y rather than the shifted-origin method — picking the wrong method here wastes most of the answer's time.

steps.label: Test the coefficients and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Comparing coefficients shows a1/a2 = b1/b2 = 1/2, so the lines 2x+y+1=0 and 4x+2y−1=0 are parallel.
steps.memory_tip: Equal ratios of x and y coefficients means: substitute the linear combination itself, here v = 2x + y.
lines: So take the substitution 2x + y = v
steps.why: When the ratio of x-coefficients equals the ratio of y-coefficients, both linear expressions are proportional to the same combination of x and y, so treating that whole combination as one new variable v turns the equation into one with a single unknown.
common_mistakes: Comparing 4x + 2y − 1 with a1x + b1y + c1 instead of a2x + b2y + c2, swapping which is which.
Missing that a1/a2 = b1/b2 here and instead attempting the shifted-origin method, which does not work in this case.

steps.label: Reduce to a function of the new variable
steps.margin_note: One mark. Differentiate v = 2x + y to relate dv/dx to dy/dx, then substitute into (1).
steps.memory_tip: v = 2x + y gives dv/dx = 2 + dy/dx, so dy/dx = dv/dx − 2.
steps.why: Differentiating the substitution v = 2x + y gives a direct relation between dv/dx and dy/dx, which replaces dy/dx everywhere in (1) and leaves an equation purely in v and x.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the derivative of 2x contributes a 2 when differentiating v = 2x + y.
Writing dy/dx = dv/dx + 2 instead of dv/dx − 2, a sign slip.

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Combine the two fractions on the right over the common denominator (2v − 1).
steps.memory_tip: 2(2v − 1) − (v + 1) = 3v − 3 = 3(v − 1) — the numerator simplifies to a clean multiple of (v − 1).
steps.why: Combining the two right-hand terms into a single fraction gives dv/dx as a clean function of v, and inverting turns the equation into a separated form where x is isolated on one side.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to invert dv/dx = (...) into dx = (...) dv when separating.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Split (2v − 1)/(v − 1) into a whole number plus a simple fraction before integrating.
steps.memory_tip: 2v − 1 = 2(v − 1) + 1 — always rewrite the numerator around the denominator's own bracket.
steps.why: Rewriting the top-heavy fraction as a constant plus a simple 1/(v−1) piece splits the integral into a plain term and a standard log term, which together give x as an explicit function of v.
common_mistakes: Trying to integrate (2v − 1)/(v − 1) directly as a log without first splitting off the constant 2.
Losing the factor of 1/3 that sits in front of the whole integral.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Multiply by 3, substitute v = 2x + y, and collect terms.
steps.memory_tip: 3x = 2v + log(v − 1) + c, then v = 2x + y turns 2v into 4x + 2y — watch the x terms combine.
lines: ⇒ 3x = 2v + log(v − 1) + c, and putting v = 2x + y:
steps.why: Multiplying through by 3 clears the fraction, substituting v = 2x + y returns the equation to the original variables, and collecting the x terms on one side gives the compact final relation the examiner expects.
common_mistakes: Losing the constant relabelling from 3c to c after multiplying the whole equation by 3.
Combining 3x − 4x incorrectly and getting the sign of x wrong in the final line.
